chapter_theme: Ujjayini's king Asokan sees a white hair, argues from the fleeting of youth and the ripening of merit, crowns his son Yasodharan and takes renunciation before Gunadhara; Yasodharan, proud of wealth, forgets dharma and gives himself to conquest and pleasure, and on the night with Amritamati a song from the elephant stable moves her heart.

cast.role: King of Ujjayini, father of Yasodharan, who sees a white hair and renounces
Asokan's son, who is crowned king of Ujjayini
the son born to Yasodharan and Amritamati
the sage before whom Asokan takes renunciation

74.reading: The poet places the story in Ujjayini, a city in the country of Avanti, which has rich fields and many towns and whose harvest even the gods desire.

75.reading: A strong elephant-riding king named Asokan lives in unbroken joy with his queen Chandramati.
75.nuance: The line calls him Indra-like in power (இந்திரனெனும் திறல்); the epic's later kings are measured against this picture of a content, untroubled house.
75.event: King Asokan lives happily with his queen Chandramati.

76.reading: Chandramati bears a son, like the young moon, and the famed father gives him the name Yasodharan, he who removes sorrow.
76.nuance: The name is spelt இசோதரன் here and யசோதரன் in verse 83; the poet glosses it as the one who removes my sorrow.
76.event: Chandramati bears a son and the father names him Yasodharan.

77.reading: The son grows up unharmed like a young elephant or lion cub, is spoken of as king, and weds Amritamati by the marriage rite, to his joy.
77.nuance: மன்னனாய் ('becoming king') comes six verses before the crowning in verse 83, so it can only mean that he is of royal standing here; the verse does not make Asokan step down yet.
77.event: The grown prince Yasodharan marries Amritamati by the wedding rite.

78.reading: As Yasodharan goes in desire to the young woman for the fruit of her beauty and breasts, the bangled wife bears a son called Yasomati, to the joy of the kin.
78.nuance: The young woman is not named here; she is read as Amritamati from verse 77.
78.event: Amritamati bears Yasodharan a son, Yasomati.

79.reading: One day the king, looking at his own form in the mirror held before him, sees with alarm a single white hair on the crown of his head.
79.nuance: The sign of age comes by sight, in a mirror held up by an attendant, and not by any teacher's word; it is the whole occasion of his turning in the next verses.
79.event: Asokan, looking in a mirror, finds a white hair on his crown and is distressed.

80.reading: The king says that this old age has come so that women with bodies like young shoots will draw away at the sight, and then even the bee-strung bow of the bodiless one is of no use to men.
80.nuance: The reasoning is entirely about desire: age is what he fears for its effect on pleasure; he does not yet speak of death or rebirth.
80.event: Asokan speaks of his old age and the uselessness of Kama's arrows to the old.

claims.claim: old age takes away the body's beauty and so the use of Kama's arrows

81.reading: The king says that youth is of this nature, so why set the mind on it in prosperity; kin are the same, and the right thing now is to leave the bond that grips the mind.
81.nuance: Speech continues from verse 80; the speaker is known from the story, with no new name here. He is speaking to himself.
81.event: Asokan reasons his way to leaving his bonds.

claims.claim: youth and kinship are fleeting and the mind should not rest on them
the fitting course is to let go of the bonds of the mind

82.reading: The king reasons that the good deeds of former births have now sprouted into wealth and thought, and that if one strives three times as much in merit one may win even Indra's world.
82.nuance: Renunciation is argued here by the profit of merit, a heaven to be won, not by release; the verse stops without a closing stop and runs into verse 83.
82.event: Asokan reasons that his past good deeds bore this wealth and that more merit would earn a heaven.

claims.claim: good deeds of a former birth sprout as present wealth
greater merit now wins the world of Indra

83.reading: Having thought thus, the king crowns his son Yasodharan lord of the land and goes, while his queen Chandramati laments.
83.nuance: The cost of the departure is set beside it: the queen's lament. The verse does not say whether she goes with him or stays.
83.event: Asokan crowns Yasodharan and leaves, and Chandramati weeps.

84.reading: Asokan bows to the sage Gunadhara, takes the vow of austere renunciation together with fifty-two kings, and goes to the forested mountain.
84.nuance: A king's renunciation is shown as a public act taken before a teacher and in company, not as a flight alone.
84.event: Asokan takes ascetic vows from Gunadhara with fifty-two kings and enters the forest hills.

85.reading: Yasodharan, in jewels, lord of Ujjayini, a jewel on his region of the earth, takes up the guard of the world under the gem-set umbrella.
85.event: Yasodharan takes up the rule of Ujjayini.

86.reading: The prince, pressed hard by the pride of wealth, becomes a heart tossed like a sea in a gale, and in an anger that overflows he turns his words and thought to desire for gain and pleasure and forgets the way of virtue.
86.nuance: After his father's reasoning in 81 the son does the opposite at once; the poet names the cause as the pride of wealth.
86.event: Pride of wealth drives Yasodharan to forget dharma for wealth and pleasure.

claims.claim: pride in wealth makes a ruler forget the way of virtue

87.reading: Fearless, the king marches on his foes, plans many deceits, lays up wealth and land, and stays a sleepless watcher who carries out what he has decided.
87.event: Yasodharan campaigns, schemes and gathers wealth with unsleeping care.

88.reading: He enjoys the sweetness of songs set to strings by women with flower garlands and watches the dance of the women who bend like lightning in the play of lovers' sulking, and some days pass.
88.event: Yasodharan spends days in song and dance among women.

89.reading: One day, sending the kings to their homes, he goes to a cool jewelled upper room of his palace, curtained all round, with a fragrant couch, and rests happily as chowries are fanned.
89.nuance: The word at line 4 is split (ருந்தான் for இருந்தான்).
89.event: Yasodharan sends the kings home and lies in the palace upper room.

90.reading: Amritamati comes to the bed with anklets and bees singing, jewels on her hips ringing, and her garland and hair hanging down.
90.event: Amritamati joins the king in the bed-room.

91.reading: As she joins him, the flood of arrows of Kama overwhelms them, they embrace and do not part, and the two become one on the scented bed.
91.event: The king and Amritamati make love.

92.reading: The king drowns in a sea of unbounded pleasure, drinking the honey of her lips and enjoying her breasts, her hips a serpent's hood for his bed.
92.nuance: இடங்கழிந்து ('beyond bounds') marks the pleasure as excess in the poet's own word, in the same scene that lists its delights.
92.event: Yasodharan is lost in pleasure with Amritamati.

93.reading: The king and the lady, in the anger of desire reversed, drain one another of their old beauty, and their eyes close in sleep.
93.event: The king and Amritamati fall asleep after love.

94.reading: From beside the elephant stable a song rises and enters her ear from afar; Amritamati wakes slowly, wonders, and melts like wax in fire.
94.nuance: The singer is not named in this verse; the song itself acts on her, so the verse sets the sound against the guarded room.
94.event: A song from the elephant stable wakes Amritamati, who melts at it.

95.reading: Her heart flows to the song, and she thinks that the joy fit for women, nectar to that lord, is in the sky for her; sighing, she cannot go on, and the king's queen stays bewildered.
95.nuance: The verse reports her thought and does not call it a fault; the phrase மதிமயக்கு ('bewilderment of mind') is the poet's word for it.
95.event: Amritamati, stirred by the song, sits in a bewildered state, sighing.

links.note: The white hair seen in the mirror is the cause of the king's crowning of his son and departure.
links.teaches: The poem lets one sign of age carry a whole renunciation, so the choice to leave is the king's own and no teacher's.

links.note: In both works a king's own greying body is held up as the plain proof that youth does not last.
links.teaches: In the Silappathikaram a sage says the king need not be told since he sees his grey frame, whereas Asokan draws the conclusion himself and acts on it.

links.note: Naladiyar praises those who renounce in childhood for foreseeing grey hair; Asokan renounces only after he sees it.
links.teaches: The king meets the Naladiyar's test late but still before the staff, so renunciation after the first white hair counts as wise, not foolish.

gains.a: The epic gets a measure for the king's timing: the quatrain says the wise act before grey hair, and he acts only at the first strand.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning of the staff gets a person who is shown acting at the first strand, which the verse alone never describes.

links.note: Both set grey hair and the loss of women's regard against the pleasure of Kama.
links.teaches: The Siddhar's youth who spends everything on women ends with a staff in his hand, while Asokan reads his first white hair in time to leave, so the two verses show the same fall averted and unaverted.

gains.a: The king's fear that women will turn away gets the full course of a man who ignored it, which the verse only hints at.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ruined youth gets a counter-case, a man who is warned by the first sign and leaves.

links.note: Both argue that the days before age are few and that austerity should be taken up before it arrives.
links.teaches: The Saiva verse points to the mountain of great austerity as the use of youth, while Asokan turns to the forest mountain and has no god to appeal to, only the fleeting of youth and kin.

gains.a: Asokan's leaving gets a Saiva statement of the same urgency, with a named goal of austerity beside the forest mountain.
gains.b: Tirumular's advice to hurry gets a case of a king who actually hands over the throne and goes.

links.note: The father leaves because youth and kin do not last; the son, once king, lives for wealth and pleasure.
links.teaches: The father's lesson on impermanence does not pass to the son, so the story shows wisdom as personal and not inherited.

links.note: Kural 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue; verse 86 says the cause: pride of wealth turns the prince to forget it.
links.teaches: The Kural names forgetting as the worst loss but not its cause, and the epic gives it as the pride of wealth.

gains.a: The verse's forgetting of dharma gets named as the ruin greater than any other.
gains.b: The couplet's forgetting gets a cause, the swelling pride of wealth in a young king.

links.note: The king's plunge into a sea of pleasure is set beside the quatrain's lamb eating the garland before its slaying.
links.teaches: The epic scene only lists pleasure's delights and the quatrain adds the shadow of the slaughter ground over them.

gains.a: The scene of delight gets the foreboding the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: The lamb image gets a concrete king, wealthy and at ease, who is as unaware as the lamb.

links.note: Amritamati in a guarded palace chamber is moved by a song from the stable: the confinement fails and her own steadfastness is the real guard.
links.teaches: The Kural says that only a woman's own steadfastness guards her, and the epic shows the guard fails through the ear, not the door, so steadfastness is a matter of the mind.

gains.a: Her wavering gets read against a test the Kural states: guarding is by the self, and her self is the one that gives way.
gains.b: The couplet's claim gets a case where walls hold and the guard within breaks at a voice.

source_issues: Verse 82 ends without a closing stop and runs on into verse 83.
Verse 83, line 4: 'மதிமதி' appears to be a doubled form of Chandramati's name.
Verse 86, line 4: 'அறத்திற மறத்து றந்தான்' is hard to divide; read here as 'forgot the way of virtue'.
Verse 89, line 4: 'ருந்தான்' is இருந்தான் in broken word division.
